On some occasion soon by July we will parade Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., March 24, 1920 Camp Commander Camp Lewis, Washington Sir: Some of our Indian boys are desirous of enlisting in the army; two have already enlisted within the last week. Inasmuch as these boys have been entrusted to my care, I feel that it is my duty to ask you to delay the enlistment of these boys until they can secure permission from their parents. I desire to call your attention to the enlistment of Boyd Eagle who joined the 35th Infantry, Company F, last week. Our records show this boy to be sixteen years of age. This age record is correct as I have a copy of the Colville census which shows the date of his birth to be 1904. I have also his application for enrollment which is signed by his father, dated September 13, 1917, which shows his age to have been twelve years at that time. As there is a likelihood that some of our boys may not give you their correct age, I would appreciate your co-operation in securing some evidence as to their correct ages before their enlistment has been made. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. OHK:MG CASE RECORD. NAME: Boyd Eagle Sex: Male Tribe: Nez Perce State: Idaho Date: Sept. 15, 1919 Age: 15 years Height: 5 ft. 4 1/2 ins. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., March 23, 1920 Officer in Charge U. S. Army Recruiting Office Tacoma, Washington Sir: Some of our Indian boys are desirous of enlisting in the army; two have already enlisted within the last week. Inasmuch as these boys have been entrusted to my care, I feel that it is my duty to ask you to delay the enlistment of these boys until they can secure permission from their parents. I desire to call your attention to the enlistment of Boyd Eagle who joined the 35th Infantry, Company F, last week. Our records show this boy to be sixteen years of age. This age record is correct as I have a copy of the Colville census which shows the date of his birth to be 1904. I have also his application for enrollment which is signed by his father, dated September 18, 1917, which shows his age to have been twelve years at that time. As there is a likelihood that some of our boys may not give you their correct age, I would appreciate your co-operation in securing some evidence as to their correct ages before their enlistment has been made. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. OHK:MG 35 Inf Co F April 24 1920 Dear Friend, Well I am going to write to you and ship Adamas just mentioned about his money what he supposed to get that $15,000 and well now's everything over there in Cushman School well, you know why we are here well you know the copper mines here well the I.W.W. and Bolshevick went on strike and they been killing all the policemen here and some wounded and the sheriff's about 8 of them been killing them and that was some fight he say them I.W.W.s were going to blow me up when we were about to arrive on train across the bridge well the sheriff caught them and they didn't make it well they all stopped and about 1100 of them working now out the rest 600 are laying around well we had a talk about them if they don't work that we ought to sent them out of this town well lot of them soldiers so said that if we only kill half of them maybe then the rest will work but the I.W.W. said they were going all work in two days well I don't know how long we are going to stay here at Butte I was on guard three of us cushman boys chasing I.W.W.s around with a bayonet oh oh. April 24, 1920 Well we are not on duty today and tomorrow we might be on Monday. Well we can't walk around town yet till after the trouble is over. Well I will close. Be sure to send Ambrose check after 15.00. From Boyd Eagle ADDRESS Capt. Boyd Eagle 35th Inf. Co. 4, Florence Hotel Butte, Montana. March 24, 1920 Dear Friend: Well I am going to drop a few words about that money well us it there now & want it as soon as its there please sent it over well I haven't time to write any more but will later let you know I am well and happy and showed them that I can drill so in oh OK and I have to go up to show walking so I'll close. From Boyd. Please send Ambone Smartlove also as quick as possible so she are broke please. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 10, 1920 Boyd Eagle 35th Infantry, Co. F Camp Lewis, Washington My Friend: There is enclosed herewith my official check No. 1591 in the amount of $20.00, which represents the balance of your account at this office. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. :MG Enc. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., April 6, 1920. Mr. E. V. Peel, Special Agent In Charge, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Peel: I have your letter advising me that Boyd Eagle has without your approval enlisted in the United States Army at Camp Lewis. I regret that Boyd failed to get your approval as judging from what I have observed of him the Army is the place for him. It is true that his father is dead and his mother I believe lives on the Yakima Reservation when she is at home. As a matter of fact she wanders around considerable from one place to another. The records of this office are somewhat confusing as to Boyd's age. The census show him to be born in 1904, however the allotment rolls which is regarded as more authentic, show him to be born in 1905. Judging from his size, I am inclined to believe this is the proper year of birth. If Boyd has received the consent of his mother I know of no objection to his entering the army. However, I do not approve of his method of leaving your school. If his enlistment in the army should stand, I have no objection to you turning over any funds that may be deposited to his credit. I am returning your file in this case. Very truly yours, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent. FCM:MG Enc. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 3, 1920 Mr. Fred C. Morgan, Supt. Colville Indian Agency Nespelem, Washington Dear Mr. Morgan: A few days ago, Boyd Eagle, one of the boys from your Reservation, enlisted in the U.S. Army at Camp Lewis. He represented that he was over eighteen years of age and, without verifying his statement, he was duly enlisted. As soon as I learned that Boyd had enlisted, I looked up his records as to his birth from his enrollment card, which shows his birth to have been in 1904. Mr. Elliott, Examiner of Inheritance, had a copy of your census file in his case, which agreed with Boyd's enrollment card. I then advised the Camp Commander at Camp Lewis of what our records showed and asked him to take the necessary steps to either dismiss Boyd from the Army or secure the consent of his parents. I am now in receipt of a letter from Boyd in which he states that he is to be dismissed from the Army. He evidently feels very much disappointed in the matter. I enclose his letter for your information. Kindly return it to me in your reply. Morgan, 2. I do not think it advisable to give him the money that he asks for, without first securing your consent thereto. Very respectfully, [signature] Special Agent in Charge. OHK:MG Enc. P.S. The enclosed correspondence from Camp Lewis was received since writing the above. Kindly return it with your reply to my letter. Put. Boyd Eagle 35th Infantry Co. F. Camp Lewis Washington Dear Friend, Well I am writing you a letter as I have heard that you wrote to the Company Commander here at Camp Lewis and that he said "that" I wasn't 18 years of age well I did tell the truth and told him that I am over 17 years and under the consent of my mother and that it was alright for me. Stay here at Camp Lewis Washington in the U.S. Army well I told the Company and that if you are going to swear over here that I am not 18 its alright I sang to enlist at any time this year so I failed three times and that I thought I was going to stay here but I am not now as usual and if you want me back you better come well that money I asked you for last Wednesday so today I am asking you to send that $20.00 right away I need that money now so please send it immediately. Your truly & friend: And if Boyd Eagle and if you want to swear that I can't stay here any longer and if I go out of the Army "believe me" Ambrose S. is coming along too if he ain't going to come I'm going to stay here, if you will shoot me down so answer and Sent the money because I want to serve my time in the U.S. Army not to tell lies. 201 (Eagle, Boyd) 5th Ind. Personally appeared before me, the Boyd Eagle, Private Company "F", 35th Infantry, who, being duly sworn, deposes and says: I was born September 11, 1901, at Fort Lapwai, Idaho, and have been at the Cushman Indian School since September, 1917. C.V. Peel has been in charge of the school since January 1, 1920; Deponent further deposes and says: My father is dead so I wrote to my mother telling her that I was going to enlist in the army, and she said that it would be all right, since I was attending a government school. I felt that I could serve myself and country better by enlisting in the army. Boyd Eagle BOYD EAGLE PRIVATE COMPANY "F" 35th INF. Subscribed and sworn to before me this 31st day of March, 1920. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or dead, this must be given. The person who signs the certificate giving to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. The laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. This form is to be used only in transfers from reservations or Indian schools to nonreservation schools. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., March 12, 1920 Fred C. Morgan, Supt. Colville Indian Agency Nezpelem, Washington Dear Sir: Boyd Eagle has requested me to write to you for the transfer of $20.00 to his credit at this office. If it is agreeable to you, I respectfully recommend the transfer. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. :MC Colville Indian Agency, Nespelem, Wash., Jan. 28, 1920 Mr. Boyd J. Magle, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear friend; I have your letter of January 24, 1920, and I am glad to hear from you. I am sorry that you do not feel well, but I am sure that if you work hard at your studies and play hard during the periods of recreation, you will be happy, and your health will be as good as possible. You inquire regarding Moses Broncheau. He is seen occasionally around Nespelem, but is not at the Agency any longer. He served a sentence imposed upon him by the Indian Court, and I believe he is now behaving himself. I note that you request $45.00 for clothing, and upon reference to your ledger account, P-62, I find that you have a balance to your credit of $247.58. On September 12, when you started to school, this fall, $40.00 was drawn on this account, and on October 30, $25.00 additional was drawn. If Mr. Peel recommends that you be allowed $45.00 additional, I shall be glad to consider this matter further, but we must all remember that a bank account that is not growing, will surely be exhausted if subjected to a steady drain, and if you can get along without an expensive overcoat for the remainder of the winter, I believe that you will get more satisfaction by using your money in some other way at a later date. I want you to be happy and well, and to get all possible good you can from the balance of the school year at Cushman. It is pleasant that you like your disciplinarian, and it is a very good plan for to hope to attend Haskell Institute next year. Mr. Peel will be very glad to consult with you about this, I am sure, and if you will tell him just what you are thinking about, I am sure he will give you helpful ideas. I hear occasionally from the other Colville boys at Cushman, and recently Patsy Moses wrote me, and from all reports the boys are doing very well. The basket ball at the Agency hall is being carried on by the returned students who are still here, Eddie Moses, James Yamout and others who live near the Agency. I am always glad to hear from you, and remember that I shall take further action on your request for money, upon receipt of word from Mr. Peel, as to his recommendation. With best wishes, I am Very truly your friend, (Sgd) Fred C Morgan, Superintendent. RS:AJ CC Mr. Peel Mr. Keller, I suggest we ask Mr. Morgan for about $20 G.T. That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions which have been promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: Boyd Eagle, a self-confessed deserter from your school residing at Spaulding, Idaho, and allotted on this reservation, came to the Agency today and requested to be advised as to whether or not he was expected to return to school. After some persuasion he finally consented to return provided I would write you a letter and recommend that leniency be shown in his case. I assured him you would be as lenient as such cases justified and that he must return with the other boys and girls who leave tomorrow. Boyd desires to purchase a new suit of clothes so I will mail you a check in the sum of forty dollars during the next few days. Very truly yours, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent FCM/MG P.S.: One of the levers I used to get Boyd to return was the promise that you would purchase a new suit of clothes for him, so I am enclosing check in the sum of $40 for that purpose. My Dear Doctor: Boyd Eagle Nesbit has again deserted. He has been traced as far as the Naches Valley, Yakima but was lost. Boyd was spanked by his officers for frightening the girls in the Domestic Science building by entering their basement through the steam tunnel. He stayed on however, until his mother managed to send him a few dollars. If he shows up, I would appreciate your holding him until I can send for him if he has sufficient funds to pay the cost of returning him to school. Thanking you, I am, Sincerely yours, Superintendent. From mother & Mabel Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dec. 9, 1918. Mr. John Sam, Auburn, Washington, Care of Mr. Chas. A. Reynolds. Dear Sir: I have written and telegraphed to the Superintendent of the Yakima Agency to hold Celestine and his runaway mate until I could send for them. He informed me that your son had gone after Celestine and he had heard that he had returned with the two boys. If this is true, both boys should be sent back immediately to the Cushman School. If your son has not gone for the boys, Mr. Carr, the Superintendent, will hold them until I can send for them. Owing to the prevalence of Influenza in that part of the country, it is not wise for you or your son to leave home and go to Yakima, as you will bring back with you the disease. St Xavier Montana Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Nov. 13, 1918. Mrs. Carrie Wesbit, St. Xavier, Montana. Dear Madam: In reply to your wire of the 11th instant received yesterday relative to Boyd Eagle, I am pleased to advise you that he has not been ill. I regret to advise that Boyd ran away from school on November 3rd in company with a Yakima boy who had previously deserted taking another boy with him and left him in the Wenatchee Valley. It is quite likely that that is where they went this time, and are likely picking apples or digging potatoes. We have not been able to get trace of the boys as yet. Please notify me promptly if you learn of his whereabouts that he may be returned. Yours very sincerely, Superintendent EHH-S Hardin Mont Nov. 11 Tacoma, Washington Please I want to know if Boyd Eagle very sick yet. Answer right away to St. Xavier, Mont Carrie Nesbit.
